title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows a general-purpose AI coding and agent tool being used as operational infrastructure inside a ransomware campaign. The Aurora group ran Cursor Agent, which itself calls Claude Sonnet, to carry out hands-on intrusion tasks including network scanning, privilege enumeration, and authentication attacks against target organizations running ESXi environments. The tool was not subverted or jailbroken in any way the reporting establishes, it was simply used as an attacker would use any capable automation tool, directing it toward malicious tasks.

The failure mode here is not a flaw in the AI model's outputs in isolation. It is the absence of controls that would distinguish malicious operator intent from legitimate use when the commands themselves, network scanning and credential testing, overlap with ordinary security and administrative work. The attacks against ten organizations proceeded across multiple months before detection by external threat researchers, not by the tool's developer or any built-in monitoring.

What is not established is whether Cursor or Anthropic had any knowledge of this use, whether any terms-of-service enforcement mechanism was triggered, or whether the seven or ten victim figures represent confirmed breaches rather than attempted intrusions. The reporting is from security vendors and journalists, not from any legal or regulatory finding.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's threat intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group has been actively targeting ESXi environments since April 2026. The group developed a Linux variant of their ransomware that encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Between April and May 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks across ten target organizations. The agent assisted with various tasks including network scanning, privilege enumeration, and authentication attacks, though many commands initially failed and required refinement.

In a separate discovery, researchers identified a second Aurora cluster operating across eight victim organizations in multiple countries. This cluster used different tactics, including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. The investigation revealed multiple infrastructure indicators including command and control servers, proxy IPs, and the group's onion-based victim negotiation portal. Gambit Security published these technical details and indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware campaigns.
